'''Robert Willis Hellwarth''' (December 10, 1930 – January 20, 2021) was an American physicist and electrical engineer who studied [[quantum electronics]], [[nonlinear optics]], and [[photonics]]. He is known for the invention of [[Q-switching]], a technique that produces short, intense pulses of laser light, and for work on [[optical phase conjugation]] and nonlinear optical processes.

==Early life and education==
Hellwarth was born December 10, 1930, in [[Ann Arbor, Michigan]], the son of Arlen Roosevelt Hellwarth, an electrical engineer, and Sarah Townsend Hellwarth.<ref name="DapkusMemorial">{{cite book |last=Dapkus |first=Paul Daniel |chapter=Robert W. Hellwarth 1930–2021 |title=Memorial Tributes: National Academy of Engineering Volume 24 |publisher=National Academy of Engineering |pages=171–176 |url=https://www.nae.edu/280856/ROBERT-W-HELLWARTH-19302021 |access-date=2026-05-20}}</ref> He grew up in [[Detroit]] and attended public schools, including [[Cooley High School]]; he was offered a scholarship to [[Princeton University]].<ref name="DapkusMemorial" /> He graduated from Princeton University in 1952 as [[valedictorian]] with a dual B.S. in electrical engineering and physics.<ref name="DapkusMemorial" /><ref name="PAWHellwarth2021">{{cite web |title=Robert W. Hellwarth '52 |website=Princeton Alumni Weekly |date=2021-05-01 |url=https://paw.princeton.edu/memorial/robert-w-hellwarth-52 |access-date=2026-05-20}}</ref> He next attended [[St John’s College, Oxford]] as a [[Rhodes Scholar]], where he joined the [[Clarendon Laboratory]] and earned a Ph.D. in physics in 1955.<ref name="DapkusMemorial" /><ref name="PAWHellwarth2021" /><ref name="RhodesHellwarth">{{cite web |year=2021 |title=Robert W. Hellwarth obituary |url=https://www.rhodeshouse.ox.ac.uk/media2/4poncasa/robert-w-hellwarth.pdf |publisher=Rhodes House}}</ref> His doctoral dissertation was titled ''An Investigation of Hyperfine Structure Using the Atomic Beam Magnetic Resonance Method''.<ref name="DapkusMemorial" />

==Career==
After completing his graduate work at Oxford, Hellwarth took a position at [[Hughes Aircraft Company]] in [[Culver City]]; he subsequently worked at [[HRL Laboratories|Hughes Research Laboratories]] in [[Malibu, California|Malibu]], and managed their Theoretical Studies Department, while holding appointments at Caltech.<ref name="DapkusMemorial" /><ref name="PAWHellwarth2021" />

Hellwarth coauthored a 1957 paper on the [[Schrödinger equation]] and [[maser]] amplifiers and oscillators.<ref name="FeynmanVernonHellwarth1957">{{cite journal |last1=Feynman |first1=Richard P. |last2=Vernon |first2=Frank L. Jr. |last3=Hellwarth |first3=Robert W. |title=Geometrical representation of the Schrödinger equation for solving maser problems |journal=Journal of Applied Physics |year=1957 |volume=28 |pages=49–52 |doi=10.1063/1.1722572}}</ref> He later coauthored a 1962 paper on electron transport in polar crystals that helped develop the concept of a [[polaron]].<ref name="FeynmanHellwarth1962">{{cite journal |last1=Feynman |first1=R. P. |last2=Hellwarth |first2=R. W. |last3=Iddings |first3=C. K. |last4=Platzman |first4=P. M. |title=Mobility of slow electrons in a polar crystal |journal=Physical Review |year=1962 |volume=127 |issue=4 |pages=1004–1017 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.127.1004}}</ref> 

He moved to the [[University of Southern California]] in 1971 as professor of electrical engineering and physics, where he became the George Pfleger Professor of Electrical Engineering and professor of physics and astronomy until his retirement in 2018.<ref name="DapkusMemorial" />

==Research and inventions==
Hellwarth worked in the fields of quantum electronics, nonlinear optics, and photonics.<ref name="DapkusMemorial" /> 

Q-switching, which Hellwarth co-invented with F.J. McClung at [[Hughes Research Laboratories]] in 1961–62, increased laser pulse power by a factor of approximately one million.<ref name="DapkusMemorial" /><ref name="Bell2021" /> Applications of Q-switched lasers include tattoo removal, surgical procedures, metal cutting, and research into laser-induced nuclear fusion.<ref name="DapkusMemorial" /><ref name="Bell2021" />

At USC, Hellwarth focused on nonlinear optical processes, devices, and materials, including work on [[four-wave mixing]] that led to the development of [[optical phase conjugation]]; this work was relevant to correction of astronomical images distorted by atmospheric fluctuations.<ref name="DapkusMemorial" /><ref name="Bell2021">{{cite web |last=Bell |first=Susan |title=Robert Hellwarth, pioneer in laser technology, dies at 90 |website=USC Dornsife News |date=2021-02-05 |url=https://dornsife.usc.edu/news/stories/in-memoriam-robert-hellwarth/ |access-date=2026-05-20}}</ref>

The description of his work that led to his election to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] mentions contributions to early laser developments at Hughes Research Laboratories and to photonics and astronomical instrumentation.<ref name="AmAcadHellwarth">{{cite web |title=Robert Willis Hellwarth |website=American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/robert-willis-hellwarth |date=April 2025 |access-date=2026-05-21}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
Source:<ref name="DapkusMemorial" />
* Member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (1977)
* Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (1986)<ref name="NASHellwarth">{{cite web |title=Robert W. Hellwarth |website=National Academy of Sciences |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/robert-w-hellwarth-fsaihp/ |access-date=2026-05-20}}</ref>
* Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (1982)
* Fellow of the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]]
* Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (1983)
* Fellow of the [[Optical Society of America]] (1987) and received their [[Charles Hard Townes Award]] in 1983 
* Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2006)<ref name="AmAcadHellwarth" />
* Received the IEEE Quantum Electronics Award in 1985
